Benchmarks

Source: vignettes/articles/benchmarks.Rmd
benchmarks.Rmd

This article measures zuroar against two other ways of keeping a set of whole numbers in R: a plain integer vector with base R’s union(), intersect() and %in%, and a bit vector from the bit package. Every number below is measured when the site is built, on whatever machine builds it, so read the tables for their shape rather than their exact values.

library(zuroar)
library(bit)
library(bench)

The sets

Values are drawn from 0 to 10 million minus one. A bit vector needs that whole universe up front; it stores value v at position v + 1. Three kinds of set show where each representation is strong:

  • dense: half of the universe, chosen at random;
  • sparse: one value in a thousand, chosen at random;
  • runs: twenty long stretches of consecutive values.
set.seed(2026)
universe <- 1e7
sets <- list(
  dense = sort(sample(universe, universe / 2) - 1L),
  sparse = sort(sample(universe, universe / 1000) - 1L),
  runs = sort(unique(unlist(lapply(
    seq(0, universe - 400000, length.out = 20),
    function(start) as.integer(start) + 0:199999
  ))))
)
lengths(sets)
#>   dense  sparse    runs 
#> 5000000   10000 4000000

as_bit <- function(v) {
  b <- bit(universe)
  b[v + 1L] <- TRUE
  b
}

Memory

The size of each representation of the first set of each pair. For zuroar, roar_stats() reports the bytes CRoaring’s containers allocate. object.size() of a bitmap reports what it would take expanded, eight bytes a value, because R sees a vector of that length.

memory <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sets), function(name) {
  v <- sets[[name]]
  data.frame(
    set = name,
    values = length(v),
    integer_vector = as.numeric(object.size(v)),
    bit = as.numeric(object.size(as_bit(v))),
    zuroar = sum(roar_stats(roar(v))$bytes)
  )
}))
memory
#>      set  values integer_vector     bit  zuroar
#> 1  dense 5000000       20000048 1251512 1253376
#> 2 sparse   10000          40048 1251512   20000
#> 3   runs 4000000       16000048 1251512     486

Operations

Each benchmark pairs a set with another of the same kind, drawn the same way. Inputs are built before timing, so only the operation is measured: the union and the intersection, each returning a new set, and a membership test of 10,000 values. mem_alloc counts only memory R allocates; CRoaring allocates its containers with C’s malloc(), which bench does not see, so zuroar’s column understates its memory. The memory table above is the fair comparison of sizes.

other <- list(
  dense = sort(sample(universe, universe / 2) - 1L),
  sparse = sort(sample(universe, universe / 1000) - 1L),
  runs = sets$runs + 100000L
)
probe <- sample(universe, 10000) - 1L

run <- function(name) {
  a <- sets[[name]]
  b <- other[[name]]
  ra <- roar(a)
  rb <- roar(b)
  ba <- as_bit(a)
  bb <- as_bit(b)
  marks <- bench::mark(
    `union: base` = union(a, b),
    `union: bit` = ba | bb,
    `union: zuroar` = ra | rb,
    `intersect: base` = intersect(a, b),
    `intersect: bit` = ba & bb,
    `intersect: zuroar` = ra & rb,
    `member: base` = probe %in% a,
    `member: bit` = ba[probe + 1L],
    `member: zuroar` = roar_contains(ra, probe),
    check = FALSE,
    filter_gc = FALSE,
    min_iterations = 5,
    time_unit = "ms"
  )
  data.frame(
    set = name,
    expression = as.character(marks$expression),
    median_ms = round(as.numeric(marks$median), 3),
    mem_alloc = format(marks$mem_alloc)
  )
}
run("dense")
#>     set        expression median_ms mem_alloc
#> 1 dense       union: base   997.684  411.34MB
#> 2 dense        union: bit     0.427    1.29MB
#> 3 dense     union: zuroar     0.664   51.16KB
#> 4 dense   intersect: base   927.681  392.28MB
#> 5 dense    intersect: bit     0.411    1.22MB
#> 6 dense intersect: zuroar     0.181        0B
#> 7 dense      member: base   218.652   83.19MB
#> 8 dense       member: bit     0.053  129.62KB
#> 9 dense    member: zuroar     0.335   78.23KB
run("sparse")
#>      set        expression median_ms mem_alloc
#> 1 sparse       union: base     0.548  892.43KB
#> 2 sparse        union: bit     0.409    1.19MB
#> 3 sparse     union: zuroar     0.036        0B
#> 4 sparse   intersect: base     0.509  736.13KB
#> 5 sparse    intersect: bit     0.413    1.19MB
#> 6 sparse intersect: zuroar     0.018        0B
#> 7 sparse      member: base     0.201  284.48KB
#> 8 sparse       member: bit     0.054   78.22KB
#> 9 sparse    member: zuroar     0.446   78.23KB
run("runs")
#>    set        expression median_ms mem_alloc
#> 1 runs       union: base   206.642  271.48MB
#> 2 runs        union: bit     0.412    1.19MB
#> 3 runs     union: zuroar     0.010        0B
#> 4 runs   intersect: base   145.530  256.22MB
#> 5 runs    intersect: bit     0.410    1.19MB
#> 6 runs intersect: zuroar     0.009        0B
#> 7 runs      member: base    33.129   47.37MB
#> 8 runs       member: bit     0.053   78.22KB
#> 9 runs    member: zuroar     0.315   78.23KB

Reading the results

A bit vector is a fixed array of one bit per possible value, so its memory and its union and intersection cost depend on the universe, not on the set. It does well on dense sets and pays the whole universe for sparse ones. A plain integer vector pays four bytes a value, and base R’s set functions hash their inputs on every call. zuroar’s containers adapt to each chunk of 65,536 values, so its size follows the set’s structure: a few hundred bytes for millions of values in long runs, about two bytes a value for sparse chunks, and a fixed 8 KiB for each dense chunk of 65,536 values.

The tables, not this text, say which is faster on the machine that built this page.
